subtype: Approach: using free tools within constraints [Thinking]
passage: Parveen had empty pockets and no bank card, which ruled out most website tools. The first evening was grim. Then Parveen made a list. “Free builder and free hosting: fine. No video plugins, no shop. So what can a free site do that a paid one doesn't? Nothing special. Unless the content is better.” The project became a guide to the birds of the neighbourhood park, with careful photos and short, accurate notes on each one. Minakshi, a classmate, looked at the first page and asked, “Won't it look plain?” Parveen shrugged. “Plain is the rule now. Big pictures, clear names, nothing that slows down a phone.” It was a limit, and it decided the whole design.

qa.q: Why did Parveen choose a free site builder?
qa.a: Parveen had empty pockets and no bank card.

qa.q: What might Parveen feel about having fewer features?
qa.a: Accepting and a little proud: the limit became a design rule instead of a complaint.

qa.q: What else could Parveen do to use the limits well, and why?
qa.a: Ask a few readers whether the bird notes are clear and easy to read on a phone, since good content is the site's strength.

qa.q: How does the site look to Minakshi?
qa.a: Minakshi worries that it will look plain, but the clear names and large pictures help visitors find what they need quickly.

grounding: With no money and no card, a teen picks free tools, accepts fewer features and puts effort into content quality.

passage:
“The good site builders all want a card, Madhav. You don't have one. So wait till college?”
“No, Ritu. There's a free builder, and free hosting. That's enough for what I want.”
“Which is?”
“Street food in our lane. Twelve stalls: what they sell, when they open, one photo each.”
“On a free plan? It'll look like everyone else's.”
“Maybe. The free plan gives me three templates and a long, ugly web address. So I'm thinking: if I can't make it fancy, I'll make it the most useful. Real photos, correct timings, the momo stall's Tuesday holiday. Nobody else has that.”
“And if you want more later?”
“Then I'll know exactly what's missing, instead of guessing now.”
Ritu leaned over the screen. “Put the chaat uncle first. His photo's the best.”

qa.q: How many stalls will the site cover?
How does Madhav seem to feel about the free plan's limits?
qa.a: Madhav seems unbothered and even determined; the limits become a reason to be useful rather than fancy.

qa.q: What else could Madhav do to make the free site stand out?
qa.a: Ask the stall owners to check their own timings and add one line each about their best dish, keeping the content accurate and personal.

qa.q: How might the stall owners see this site?
qa.a: They would likely be pleased to have correct timings and a photo online at no cost, even with a long web address.

grounding: Shows a teen with no money or card reasoning through free tools, accepting fewer features and putting the effort into accurate content.

subtype: Approach: using free tools within constraints [Thinking]
passage:
Last year I built a site for our colony's book exchange, and the first thing I learned was what zero rupees buys. I'm Dhruv. No card, no pocket money to spare, so I used a site builder that costs nothing, with hosting that was free too. That plan allowed five pages and no search box.
Jatin, who helped me collect the lists, kept saying, “Without search, nobody will use it.” I nearly gave up. Then I thought: five pages, fine. One page each for Classes Eight to Twelve. If each page is short and sorted, people don't need search; they need a clean list.
So I spent my effort there, checking every title twice and removing books already given away. The limit became my rule: nothing goes on a page unless someone can pick it up this week. By June, forty-one books had changed hands.

qa.q: How many pages did the free plan allow?
qa.a: The free plan allowed five pages.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when Jatin kept saying nobody would use it without search?
qa.a: Dhruv felt discouraged enough to nearly give up, until the reasoning about short, sorted lists brought back some confidence.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv have tried if the lists grew too long for one page per class?
qa.a: Split each class page by subject within the same five pages, or ask users what they look for first before adding anything.

qa.q: How might Jatin see the site after forty-one books changed hands?
qa.a: Jatin would probably admit a clean list worked without search, and feel part of the success after collecting the lists.

grounding: Shows a teen with no money using a free builder and hosting, accepting no search box and turning the page limit into a rule about content quality.
